intro.html: How much do you want to do something? English has a whole scale of words for it, from the burning eagerness of an ardent fan to the foot-dragging of a reluctant helper. Several of the eager words come from Latin words for heat: ardent from “burn,” fervent from “boil.”

Eager: zealous (devoted to a cause), ardent and fervent (burning, glowing with feeling), avid (eager for more), keen (eager; also sharp), alacrity (cheerful speed, a noun). Unwilling: reluctant (hesitant), loath (unwilling), averse (opposed, turned away), grudging (given unwillingly).

words.def: full of eager devotion to a cause or task
words.ex: The {zealous} volunteers cleaned the whole beach before breakfast.
words.ctx: Most of the club recycled when it was convenient, but Omar was {zealous} about it: he sorted every scrap, rinsed every can and reminded everyone else to do the same.
words.etym: From zeal, from Greek zelos, “eagerness, fervor.”

mn.cue: ZEAL-ous: full of ZEAL, A to Z
mn.text: Omar sorts every can, bottle and scrap of paper into the right bin and cheers each one in. His zeal for recycling makes him {zealous}.

scene.alt: A man in a headband eagerly sorts bottles into recycling bins.

words.ex: Grandma is an {ardent} baseball fan; she has not missed a home game in forty years.
words.ctx: Though his friends had lost interest in comic books, Jamal remained an {ardent} collector, hunting through yard sales every weekend for missing issues.

mn.text: Granny Mae has cheered for the home team for forty years, and her love still burns hot: cap, flag and a voice you can hear in the parking lot. She is an {ardent} fan.

scene.alt: A grandmother in a cap waves a flag and cheers her team with burning enthusiasm.

words.ex: Lila made a {fervent} wish as she blew out the candles.
words.ctx: The crowd’s applause was {fervent}: people stood, cheered and stamped their feet until the band came back for one more song.
words.etym: From Latin fervere, “to boil, to glow.”

mn.text: Lila squeezes her eyes shut and wishes so hard over her birthday candles that she glows as if she had a fever. Her wish is {fervent}.

scene.alt: A girl squeezes her eyes shut and wishes with all her heart over her birthday cake.

words.ex: Zoe is an {avid} reader who finishes a book every two days.
words.ctx: Even in the rain, the {avid} bird-watchers stayed out on the marsh for hours, binoculars raised, hoping to glimpse the rare heron.
words.etym: From Latin avidus, “eager, greedy,” from avere, “to crave.”

mn.text: The moment the new book arrives, Zoe grabs it: “I have to have it!” She has read it twice by Sunday. She is an {avid} reader.

labels.text: AV-id: I have to HAVE it!

scene.alt: A girl hugs a new book eagerly beside a tall pile of books she has already read.

words.ex: Dev was {keen} to try the new climbing wall.
words.ctx: The owl’s {keen} eyesight let it spot a mouse moving in the grass from the top of a tall pine, far across the dark field.
words.note: Keen has two common senses: eager (keen to help) and sharp (a keen knife, keen eyes, a keen mind).

mn.text: Dev, the keen teen, is first in line at the climbing rock, helmet on, an hour before it opens. He is {keen} to climb.

scene.alt: A teen in a climbing helmet bounces with eagerness at the foot of a climbing rock.

words.ex: When Mom asked who wanted ice cream, the kids answered with {alacrity}.
words.ctx: Kai usually dragged his feet at chore time, but when Grandpa asked for help building a treehouse, he agreed with {alacrity}, grabbing a hammer before Grandpa had finished asking.
words.etym: From Latin alacritas, from alacer, “lively, brisk.”

mn.text: When Grandpa asks who wants to help build the treehouse, Kai springs off the couch like an acrobat: “Me! Now!” He answers with {alacrity}.

scene.alt: A boy springs up eagerly from the sofa when his grandfather holds up a hammer.

words.ex: The {reluctant} puppy had to be carried into the bath.
words.ctx: Ivy was {reluctant} to jump off the high dive: she climbed the ladder twice, peered over the edge, and climbed back down both times.
words.etym: From Latin reluctari, “to struggle against”: re (against) + luctari (to struggle).

mn.cue: re-LUCK-tant: no LUCK getting him to go
mn.text: Maya tugs Kai toward the dance floor, but he leans back with all his weight: no luck. He is {reluctant} to dance.

scene.alt: A girl tugs a boy toward the dance floor while he leans back, unwilling.

words.ex: Grandpa was {loath} to sell the old truck he had driven for forty years.
words.ctx: Though the job paid well, Nell was {loath} to take it, because it meant moving far from the friends and the garden she loved.
words.etym: From Old English lath, “hostile, hateful,” the same source as loathe.
words.note: Loath (unwilling) is an adjective; loathe (to hate) is a verb. “I am loath to go,” but “I loathe cold soup.”

mn.cue: a SLOTH is LOATH to let go
mn.text: Time to climb down? The sloth hugs its cozy branch and won’t budge an inch. A sloth is always {loath} to let go.

scene.alt: A sleepy sloth clings to its branch and refuses to come down while a girl calls it.

words.ctx: Though usually {averse} to risk, the careful banker surprised everyone by leaving his job to open a surf shop.
words.etym: From Latin aversus, “turned away”: ab (away) + vertere (to turn).
words.note: Averse (unwilling, usually followed by to) is not adverse (harmful): “averse to risk,” but “adverse weather.”

mn.text: Show Mittens the washtub, and she turns her whole body away, nose in the air. She is {averse} to baths.

scene.alt: A cat turns its back on a washtub of water while a woman holds up soap.

words.ex: Kai gave a {grudging} apology to his sister, staring at his shoes the whole time.
words.ctx: Though the critic had disliked the director’s earlier films, he offered {grudging} praise for this one, admitting that its final scene was beautiful.
words.etym: From grudge, from an old verb meaning “to grumble, to complain.”

mn.text: Mom says Kai must share, so he hands his sister half of his fudge with a scowl and a long sigh. His sharing is {grudging}.

scene.alt: A grumpy boy hands half his fudge to his happy sister.

after.html: Two sound-alike traps: loath (unwilling, an adjective) and loathe (to hate, a verb); averse (unwilling) and adverse (harmful, unfavorable). You are averse to risk; the weather is adverse.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: Grandpa was loath to sell his old truck.
Grandpa was loathe to sell his old truck.
items.why: Loath (no e) is the adjective meaning unwilling. Loathe (with an e) is the verb meaning to hate.

items.q: Which sentence uses the right word?
choices: She is averse to taking big risks.
The averse weather closed the roads.
The medicine had averse side effects.
items.why: Averse means unwilling or opposed (averse to risk). Harmful weather or side effects are adverse.

items.q: True or false: to do something with alacrity is to do it slowly and unwillingly.
items.why: False. Alacrity is cheerful readiness and speed, the opposite of dragging your feet.

items.q: The coach finally gave ______ approval to the new play, though she still had doubts. Which word fits?
items.why: Approval given unwillingly, with doubts, is grudging.
